study.locator: When the pattern bends: State-space BFS (LC 127, LC 752)
study.depth: Read only that section here. The queue mechanics belong to the BFS unit.

focus: Default to the adjacency list on sparse graphs: at \(n = 10^{5}\) the chapter's arithmetic gives about 1.6 MB for the list against about \(10^{10}\) matrix cells. Take the matrix only under \(n \le 500\) with heavy edge tests, and keep the raw edge list for Kruskal and Bellman-Ford.
An undirected edge is two adjacency entries; a directed edge is one. The directed flag belongs in the constructor, not in the traversal.
An implicit graph is a neighbor function, not a table: four lines of grid arithmetic or one-letter word mutations replace a 10,000-vertex grid build.
When the state carries more than the vertex (a word, a lock combination, keys held), the visited mark must sit on the state. Marking the bare vertex merges distinct states.
units.reproduce: From a blank file with the course Python (3.13.14), build the undirected adjacency list for \(n = 5\) and edges [(0,1),(0,2),(1,3),(2,3),(3,4)], assert adj[3] == [1,2,4], then BFS from 0 and report distances {0:0, 1:1, 2:1, 3:2, 4:3}. Then write grid_neighbors(r, c, rows, cols) yielding the four in-bounds neighbors, and state in one sentence why Word Ladder nodes are words rather than positions.
traps: Forgetting the second push for undirected edges: BFS reaches one side of an edge but not the other, and reports disconnected on a connected input.
Building an adjacency list for an edge-centric algorithm: Kruskal sorts the input edge list and Bellman-Ford scans it; neither queries neighbors of one vertex, so the build is pure overhead.
Marking the vertex instead of the state: two paths reaching the same cell with different keys collapse into one visited bit, and the second path is wrongly pruned.

selfTest.q: List, matrix or edge list for BFS on a sparse graph with \(n = 10^{5}\), and why?
selfTest.a: Adjacency list. Traversal costs \(\Theta(V + E)\) on the list against \(\Theta(V^2)\) on the matrix, and the matrix needs about \(10^{10}\) cells at that scale.

selfTest.q: LC 1557 answers with an in-degree array and no adjacency list. What is the general lesson?
selfTest.a: Store the minimum structure the algorithm consumes. In-degree-zero detection needs counts, not neighbors.

selfTest.q: Two searches reach grid cell (2,2), one holding key A and one holding nothing. One visited bit on (2,2): what breaks?
selfTest.a: The second arrival is skipped although its future differs: the doors it can open are not the same. The visited key must be (cell, keys).

selfTest.q: Why do Kruskal and Bellman-Ford take the edge list as is?
selfTest.a: They consume edges in bulk order (by weight, or all of them per pass) and never query the neighbors of one vertex.

study.title: Unweighted shortest paths by BFS
study.locator: Chapter 8, Section 8.4 Unweighted Graphs: Breadth-First Search with the FIFO queue and layer analysis (printed pp. 278-281)

focus: Mark visited at enqueue, on the same line as the push. Marking at dequeue lets several queued neighbors push the same vertex, so the queue holds up to \(E\) entries, and without a skip-on-pop check each duplicate is expanded again, up to \(\Theta(V \times E)\) work on dense graphs.
The FIFO invariant: the queue always holds vertices at most two consecutive distances from the sources. Draining a full layer before the next is what makes first discovery shortest.
Multi-source BFS seeds every source at depth 0 in one pre-scan, equivalent to a virtual super-source with zero-weight edges. One run replaces one BFS per source.
Counting is an outer scan wrapped around the traversal: every unvisited land cell starts one flood. Minutes count edges traversed; binary-matrix path length counts cells, so it adds one.
units.reproduce: From a blank file with the course Python (3.13.14), run multi-source BFS on [[2,1,1],[1,1,0],[0,1,1]] and return 4; on [[2,1,1],[0,1,1],[1,0,1]] return -1; on a grid with no fresh cells return 0. State the input size (\(3 \times 3\)) and that the answer counts edges, not cells.
traps: list.pop(0) as a queue: each pop shifts the remaining elements, so at 20,000 queued cells one pop costs about 1.9 us against about 11 ns for deque.popleft (measured on 12th Gen i9-12900K, Python 3.13.14). Always import deque.
A single-source loop over sources for a multi-source question: \(n\) runs give \(n\) single-source distances, not the parallel-frontier minimum the problem asks for.
Cell-versus-edge counting: LC 994 returns the depth of the last rotted cell while LC 1091 returns depth plus one for the cell-inclusive path. Trace a 3-cell line by hand before submitting.

selfTest.q: Prove BFS first discovery is shortest.
selfTest.a: Induction on layers: sources are distance 0, and the queue dequeues every distance-\(d\) vertex before any distance-\((d + 1)\) vertex is discovered, since discovery appends to the back. So the first edge reaching \(v\) comes from a distance-\((\operatorname{dist}(v) - 1)\) vertex along a shortest path, and no shorter path can exist or \(v\) would have been discovered earlier.

selfTest.q: Why does the super-source argument preserve the bound?
selfTest.a: The virtual source adds one vertex and one zero-weight edge per real source, scanned once in the seed pass. Total work stays \(\Theta(V + E)\).

selfTest.q: A diamond \(A \to B\), \(A \to C\), \(B \to D\), \(C \to D\) with visited marked at dequeue: what happens?
selfTest.a: \(B\) and \(C\) both see \(D\) unmarked before \(D\) is dequeued, so \(D\) is pushed twice. If the pop skips marked vertices, the answer is still right but the queue carries duplicates; if it does not, \(D\) is expanded twice. Marking at enqueue pushes \(D\) once.

selfTest.q: LC 547 reads an \(n \times n\) matrix but runs the same template as LC 200. What changes?
selfTest.a: Only the neighbor function: neighbors of \(i\) are columns \(j\) with isConnected[i][j] == 1. Cost becomes \(\Theta(n^2)\) because every matrix cell is read.

study.title: Depth-first search through cycle detection
study.locator: Sections 6.1 Preorder and Postorder (with Classifying Vertices and Edges) and 6.2 Detecting Cycles (printed pp. 227-232)

focus: Mark before recursing, on entry. Recursing first lets the neighbor immediately recurse back, which loops until RecursionError.
GRAY means on the current stack; BLACK means finished. The diamond edge into a BLACK vertex is a benign forward edge; only a GRAY neighbor is a back edge and a cycle witness.
Undirected DFS needs one boolean plus the parent argument: the neighbor you arrived from does not count. Three colors are unnecessary there because undirected DFS has no forward or cross edges.
Bipartite colors are 1 and -1 with 0 for unvisited, flipped by negation across each edge, inside an outer loop over components. A same-color edge is the odd-cycle witness.
units.reproduce: From a blank file with the course Python (3.13.14), run three-color DFS on the diamond [(0,1),(0,2),(1,3),(2,3)] and report no cycle, and on [(0,1),(1,2),(2,0)] report a cycle. Then run two-color BFS on [[1,3],[0,2],[1,3],[0,2]] (True) and on [[1,2],[0,2],[0,1]] (False).
traps: Two-color directed DFS: the diamond reports a cycle because one visited bit conflates on-stack with finished. The fix is the third color, not a second visited set.
Parentless undirected DFS: a single edge reports a cycle because each endpoint sees the other as visited. The fix is the parent argument, not more colors.

Recursive DFS on deep grids or chains: CPython caps the stack at 1000 frames by default (check with sys.getrecursionlimit), so a snake region or a 2000-chain crashes. Set the limit explicitly or ship the iterative form.

selfTest.q: Prove a directed graph is acyclic iff DFS finds no back edge.
selfTest.a: If a back edge \((u, v)\) exists, \(v\) is an ancestor of \(u\), so the tree path from \(v\) to \(u\) plus the edge closes a cycle. Conversely, if a cycle exists, let \(v\) be its first vertex DFS discovers. Every other cycle vertex is still white then, so each becomes a descendant of \(v\), and the cycle edge from \(v\)'s predecessor \(u\) back to \(v\) reaches \(v\) while \(v\) is still GRAY: a back edge.

selfTest.q: Prove a graph is bipartite iff it has no odd cycle.
selfTest.a: If 2-colored, any cycle alternates colors and must return to its start color after an even number of steps, so all cycles are even. If no odd cycle exists, BFS two-coloring never assigns the same color to both ends of an edge: a conflict would close an odd cycle through the BFS tree, contradiction.

selfTest.q: Why does the bipartite outer loop cost nothing on connected graphs?
selfTest.a: Every later start is already colored, so each trips the continue immediately: \(O(V)\) checks total. Skipping the loop misses odd cycles hiding in unvisited components.

selfTest.q: LC 130 floods from the border instead of testing each region. Why is the inversion sound?
selfTest.a: Border-connected regions are exactly the ones to keep; DFS marks all of them, so every unmarked O is surrounded by construction. Testing from inside cannot see the border without the same outward walk.

units.title: Topological ordering and strongly connected components
outcomes: Implement Kahn's algorithm and DFS post-order topological sort, each with its cycle witness, and derive the \(\Theta(V + E)\) bound.
Prove post-order-then-reverse is a topological order from the finish-time invariant.
Implement Kosaraju's strongly connected components and explain the reverse-graph second pass.
units.why: Dependency order is the scheduling primitive: builds, courses, task graphs. The same DFS skeleton that orders a DAG also carves directed graphs into strongly connected components.

next.note: Topological order is the evaluation order for DP on DAGs; carry it into recurrence dependencies.
DAG shortest paths relax vertices in topological order, which is why order comes before weights.

study.title: Topological sort: Kahn's algorithm
study.locator: What Kahn's actually does; The algorithm (LC 207); Worked example on the 6-course catalog; Reverse-graph Kahn for safe nodes (LC 802)

study.title: Topological sort: DFS post-order reverse
study.locator: Why two colors are not enough; The algorithm; Walking the canonical DAG; Why post-order, then reverse, is correct; Picking between Kahn and DFS

study.title: Topological sort and strong components
study.locator: Section 6.3 Topological Sort with Implicit Topological Sort; Sections 6.5 Strong Connectivity and 6.6 Strong Components in Linear Time, Kosaraju and Sharir's algorithm (printed pp. 232-234 and 237-244; Tarjan's algorithm is optional)

focus: Pin the edge convention in a comment: [a,b] means \(b\) is the prerequisite, so the edge is \(b \to a\). Inverting it turns DAGs into cycles.
Kahn detects the cycle only at termination: emitted count equal to \(V\) means DAG, fewer means the leftovers sit on cycles. No early return inside the loop.
DFS emits each vertex after all successors finish, so finish times decrease along every edge; reversing puts producers first. A GRAY successor aborts with a cycle.
Kosaraju finishes SCCs in topological order on the first pass, then walks the reversed graph from the latest-finishing component, which cannot escape its own SCC.
units.reproduce: From a blank file with the course Python (3.13.14), run Kahn on \(n = 6\) with [[1,0],[2,0],[3,1],[3,2],[4,2],[5,3],[5,4]] and emit a valid order such as [0,1,2,3,4,5] (check every \(b\) precedes its \(a\)); on [[1,0],[0,1]] emit 0 of 2 and report a cycle. Then run Kosaraju on [(0,1),(1,2),(2,0),(2,3),(3,4)] and report components [0,0,0,1,2].
traps: Counting indegrees from one edge collection and decrementing from another, such as a deduplicated set against the raw list with duplicate prerequisites: counts go negative or never reach zero. Count and decrement from the same list, and enqueue exactly when a count reaches 0.
Returning the post-order list unreversed: it holds consumers before producers, the exact opposite of the graded order.
Running DFS from vertex 0 only: cycles in other weakly connected components are missed. The outer white-check loop is mandatory, as is the GRAY-to-BLACK flip on exit.

selfTest.q: Prove post-order-then-reverse is a topological order.
selfTest.a: When DFS exits \(u\), its loop has returned from every successor, so each successor finished earlier: \(\operatorname{finish}[v] < \operatorname{finish}[u]\) for every edge \((u, v)\). Reversing finish-time order therefore places \(u\) before \(v\) on every edge, which is the topological property.

selfTest.q: Prove leftover vertices after Kahn imply a cycle.
selfTest.a: Every leftover vertex still has indegree at least one inside the leftover subgraph. Follow any predecessor chain; with finitely many vertices some vertex repeats, and the repeated segment is a directed cycle.

selfTest.q: Why does Kosaraju's second pass stay inside one SCC?
selfTest.a: First-pass finish times order SCCs topologically: if SCC \(A\) reaches SCC \(B\), \(A\) finishes later. Processing latest-first on the reversed graph starts each walk in a sink SCC of the reversed graph, whose reachable set is exactly its own SCC.

selfTest.q: Kahn and DFS report different valid orders on the same DAG. Is one wrong?
selfTest.a: No. Topological orders are plural: the handbook's 6-node DAG admits several. Kahn breaks ties by queue order, DFS by recursion shape; both respect every edge.

study.title: Union-Find: parent forests, path compression, and union by rank
study.locator: The forest, the find, the union; Two heuristics that change the bound; Putting it all together (LC 684); LC 990: equality and inequality, two passes
study.depth: Skim LC 685's directed case-split on first pass; return after the MST unit if directed redundancy still bites.

study.title: Disjoint Sets, Lecture Note 11
study.locator: 11.1 Reversed Trees (union by depth or rank, and the size-at-least-2-to-the-rank property); 11.3 Path Compression; 11.6 The Ackermann Function and its Inverse for the bound. Skim 11.2 Shallow Threaded Trees.

focus: Compare find(x) with find(y), never parent[x] with parent[y]: cousins share a root through a chain while their immediate parents differ.
Rank is an upper bound on height, not the height: compression shrinks trees without lowering ranks, and the size-at-least-2-to-the-rank property is what the log bound leans on.
Count components as the set of find(i) over all \(i\), never as the set of parent entries: stale intermediate pointers undercount.
Process all equalities before any inequality (LC 990): input order lies, because a later union can connect an earlier checked pair.
units.reproduce: From a blank file with the course Python (3.13.14), process [[1,2],[1,3],[2,3]] and return [2,3] as the first redundant edge. Then union the chain 0-1 through 6-7 in order with union by rank and report maximum depth 1.
traps: Rank without compression, or compression without rank: the adversarial chain union(0,1), union(1,2), ... builds depth \(n\) when attachment is one-sided, and compression never fires before the first find.
Recursive find on production-size chains: fine at LC 684 scale (\(n \le 1000\)), but the recursive form costs a frame per hop. Ship the iterative two-pass form past \(10^{5}\) elements.
String keys without make-set: integer constructors pre-fill every root, but email-keyed maps need an explicit make on first sighting or find raises KeyError.

selfTest.q: Derive the \(O(\log n)\) bound for union by rank alone.
selfTest.a: A rank-\(r\) root has at least \(2^r\) descendants (equal-rank merges double the set), so a tree on \(n\) nodes has rank at most \(\log_2 n\), and find walks at most that many parent pointers.

selfTest.q: Why do two passes decide LC 990 correctly?
selfTest.a: Pass one builds every equivalence class the equalities force. Pass two checks each inequality against the final partition: any same-set inequality contradicts the input, and no order dependence remains because all unions precede all checks.

selfTest.q: Give two queries union-find cannot answer.
selfTest.a: Deletions (parent pointers only merge; splitting needs a rebuild) and directed reachability or path queries (roots record connectivity, not direction or routes).

selfTest.q: What does \(\alpha(n) \le 4\) mean in practice?
selfTest.a: Tarjan's bound says \(m\) operations cost \(O(m \times \alpha(n))\); \(\alpha\) stays at most 4 for any storable \(n\), so every operation is effectively constant, and the 1979 lower bound says no pointer-machine structure beats it.

study.locator: The operations: pop, lazy-skip, relax, settle; Lazy deletion: pushing duplicates instead of decrease-key; Worked example with the two stale-skip events

study.locator: The algorithm, in three pieces; Why V minus 1 is the right number; Bellman-Ford with a budget: LC 787 with the snapshot line; Detecting a negative cycle

study.title: Shortest Paths, Chapter 8
study.locator: 8.1 Shortest Path Trees, 8.2 Negative Edges and 8.3 The Only SSSP Algorithm; 8.5 Directed Acyclic Graphs; 8.6 Best-First: Dijkstra's Algorithm with No Negative Edges; 8.7 Relax ALL the Edges: Bellman-Ford (printed pp. 274-296)

focus: heapq has no decrease-key (check hasattr on the course Python: False), so this card uses the lazy-deletion variant: push a fresh entry per relaxation and skip with if d > dist[u]: continue. Count the skips; the handbook graph produces exactly 2.

Settle-once holds only for nonneg weights: every undiscovered alternative path must leave through an unsettled vertex of distance at least \(d\), so adding nonneg remainders cannot beat \(d\). One negative edge breaks the argument and the code stays silent.

Bellman-Ford's pass \(i\) is correct for paths of at most \(i\) edges by induction, and simple paths use at most \(V - 1\) edges. The \(V\)th pass is the detector, not bookkeeping: any relaxation there proves a reachable negative cycle.
\(K\)-edge budgets read from the previous pass: snapshot = dist[:] each round. Reading live dist chains two edges in one pass and silently spends budget twice.
units.reproduce: From a blank file with the course Python (3.13.14): Dijkstra on the 6-node handbook graph (source 0) returns [0,7,9,20,20,11] with exactly 2 stale skips (7 pushes, 8 pops). A settle-once variant on edges [(0,1,6),(0,2,7),(2,3,-3),(3,1,-2)] locks dist[1] at 6 while Bellman-Ford reports the true 2. LC 787's sample (\(n = 4\), \(k = 1\)) returns 700 with the snapshot line and the wrong 400 without it.
traps: Negative input to Dijkstra: no exception, no warning, wrong distances. Scan weights for negatives first; one negative edge reroutes to Bellman-Ford.
\(K\) stops means \(K + 1\) edges: a direct flight is 0 stops and 1 edge. Running \(K\) passes under-relaxes by one hop.

Missing INF guard before dist[u] + w: in Java and C++ INT_MAX plus w wraps negative and relaxes the unreachable. Gate on dist[u] != INF; Python with float inf is exempt but keep the guard for portability.

selfTest.q: Prove the settle-once claim.
selfTest.a: Let \(u\) pop with the smallest tentative distance \(d\). Take any source-to-\(u\) path and let \(y\) be its first vertex outside the settled set. Its predecessor \(x\) was settled with an exact distance (induction) and relaxed \((x, y)\), so the prefix up to \(y\) costs at least \(\operatorname{dist}[x] + w(x, y) \ge \operatorname{dist}[y]\), and \(\operatorname{dist}[y] \ge d\) because \(u\) popped first. The rest of the path adds nonnegative weight, so no path beats \(d\) and \(\operatorname{dist}[u]\) is final.

selfTest.q: Prove \(V - 1\) passes suffice for Bellman-Ford.
selfTest.a: Induction: pass 1 fixes all one-edge shortest paths from direct relaxations; if pass \(i - 1\) fixed all paths of at most \(i - 1\) edges, pass \(i\) extends each by one scanned edge. Simple shortest paths repeat no vertex, hence use at most \(V - 1\) edges.

selfTest.q: Why does the no-snapshot LC 787 code return 400 instead of 700?
selfTest.a: Without the snapshot the first pass already chains edges: (0,1) sets dist[1] = 100, then (1,2) reads it and sets dist[2] = 200, then (2,3) sets dist[3] = 400, three edges against a two-edge budget. The snapshot makes every pass extend only the previous pass's distances.

selfTest.q: When is 0-1 BFS the right call over Dijkstra?
selfTest.a: All weights in \(\{{0, 1\}}\): push front on 0-cost, back on 1-cost relaxations. The deque front always holds minimum tentative distance, so each operation is \(O(1)\) and total is \(\Theta(V + E)\) instead of heap-logged.

units.title: Minimum spanning trees with Kruskal and Prim

Prove accepted edges are safe with the cut-property exchange argument, and rejected edges with the cycle property.
Choose Kruskal for explicit edge lists and Prim (dense \(O(V^2)\) or heap) for dense or implicit graphs.
units.why: Minimum connection cost is the canonical greedy-with-proof: one theorem justifies two algorithms, and the input shape picks between them.

next.note: The cut property is the exchange argument in its cleanest form; carry it into greedy correctness proofs.
Verify your MST against brute force on \(n \le 8\) before trusting the greedy.

study.title: Minimum spanning trees: Prim's algorithm
study.locator: The pattern with the in_mst skip; When the graph is implicit: LC 1584; Dense Prim from \(O(n^2 \log n)\) to \(O(n^2)\); Kruskal vs Prim: the decision table

study.title: Minimum Spanning Trees, Chapter 7
study.locator: 7.1 Distinct Edge Weights; 7.2 The Only Minimum Spanning Tree Algorithm (safe and useless edges); 7.3 Boruvka's Algorithm; 7.4 Jarnik's ("Prim's") Algorithm; 7.5 Kruskal's Algorithm (printed pp. 257-268)

focus: Kruskal's guard is union: accept iff endpoints sit in different components, stop at \(n - 1\) edges. The sort dominates at \(O(E \log E)\); the DSU loop is effectively linear.
Lazy Prim pushes (weight, vertex) pairs and skips with if in_mst[u]: continue. The heap holds duplicates; the eager decrease-key variant needs an indexed heap no standard library ships.
Prim cumulates nothing: pushing distance-from-start plus edge weight builds a shortest-path tree, not an MST. Dijkstra cumulates, Prim does not.
Every MST has the same total weight, and distinct weights also make the edge set unique. With ties, as in LC 1584, Kruskal and Prim may pick different edges but must report the same total.
units.reproduce: From a blank file with the course Python (3.13.14), run Kruskal and dense Prim on [[0,0],[2,2],[3,10],[5,2],[7,0]]; both return 20. State the input size (\(n = 5\), complete graph of 10 Manhattan edges) and which variant each function is.
traps: Early break on disconnected input: stopping is valid only when \(n - 1\) accepts happen. Otherwise walk every edge and return -1 when accepts fall short.
Integer totals in Java and C++: LC 1584 edge weights reach \(4 \times 10^{6}\) and 999 of them sum past INT_MAX. Accumulate in long or long long; Python integers are exempt.
Forgetting either DSU heuristic: one-sided chains push finds to \(O(n)\) before compression ever fires. Ship path halving with union by rank as in the handbook reference.

selfTest.q: Prove the cut property by exchange.
selfTest.a: Let \(e\) be the lightest edge across cut \((S, V - S)\) and \(T^{*}\) an MST missing \(e\). Adding \(e\) creates a cycle with another crossing edge \(e'\) of weight at least \(w(e)\). Swapping \(e'\) for \(e\) keeps a spanning tree of no greater weight, so some MST contains \(e\).

selfTest.q: Why is a rejected Kruskal edge safe to drop?
selfTest.a: Its endpoints already connect through accepted edges, each processed earlier hence no heavier. The closed cycle's other edges are all at most as heavy, so the rejected edge is a heaviest edge of that cycle and no MST needs it.

selfTest.q: Why does dense Prim beat heap Prim on LC 1584?
selfTest.a: The complete graph materializes about 500,000 edges at \(n = 1000\); heap Prim pays \(O(n^2 \log n)\) on them while dense Prim scans min_edge arrays for \(O(n^2)\) with no heap and no stale entries.

selfTest.q: Kruskal and Prim report different totals on the same input. What follows?
selfTest.a: A bug: all minimum spanning trees share one total weight, so two correct runs agree on it even when tied weights let them choose different edges. Check the stale skip, the union guard and the weight function.

units.title: Graph certificates and exhaustive small-graph validation
outcomes: Write \(O(V + E)\) checkers for claimed paths, orders and trees that use only the input plus the output.

Measure adjacency representations on matched workloads with timeit, reporting CPU, Python version and setup instead of quoting ratios.
units.why: An algorithm without an independent checker is a rumor. Certificates turn outputs into checkable claims, and generated-graph tests turn examples into evidence.

next.note: Carry the checker habit into matching: a cut of equal value certifies a flow.
Apply the same oracle discipline to recurrences: brute force on small instances first.

study.title: Floyd-Warshall as the oracle
study.locator: Section 9.8 (Kleene-Roy-)Floyd-Warshall(-Ingerman): the triple loop over intermediate vertices (printed p. 318)

focus: A certificate is checked by different code than the solver: re-walk parent pointers for distances, scan every edge against a claimed topological order, recount components. \(O(V + E)\) checkers, no shared helpers.

Generate edge lists with @composite (draw \(n\), draw \(m\), draw weighted pairs), dedupe parallel edges explicitly, and cover disconnected and cyclic shapes: the default random graph is connected-ish and hides the interesting failures.
Compare on the same instance: Dijkstra against Floyd-Warshall's row, Kruskal against Prim and against brute force at \(n \le 8\). Cross-instance numbers prove nothing.

Report measurements with setup: BFS on a seeded \(n = 3000\) sparse graph takes about 0.3 ms over the list against about 97 ms over the matrix on 12th Gen i9-12900K with Python 3.13.14. Re-run it; the direction is the claim, not the ratio, and the gap is CPython row-scan overhead, not a portable constant.
units.reproduce: From a blank file with the course Python (Hypothesis 6.169.0): a @composite small-graph strategy (\(n \le 7\), derandomize=True) comparing Dijkstra against Floyd-Warshall on nonneg weights passes 100 examples with zero disagreements. Separately, timeit on a seeded \(n = 3000\), 9,000-edge sparse graph shows BFS over the adjacency list at about 0.3 ms against about 97 ms over the matrix. Quote both numbers with CPU and Python version.
traps: Oracle and solver sharing code: two Dijkstra implementations sharing the relax helper agree even when both are wrong. The oracle must be an independent formulation (triple loop, exhaustive search).
Connected-only generation: strategies drawing \(m \ge n - 1\) edges rarely emit isolated vertices, so component and unreachable handling goes untested. Force sparse and empty draws.
Quoting the 300x ratio as a constant: it measures CPython-level matrix row scans on one CPU, not an algorithmic invariant. C++ crossover points never transfer without a local measurement.

selfTest.q: What makes a checker independent?
selfTest.a: It reads only the input and the claimed output, runs a different algorithm than the solver (edge scan, pointer re-walk), and costs \(O(V + E)\). Shared helpers or re-running the solver prove nothing.

selfTest.q: Why is Floyd-Warshall a valid oracle for Dijkstra tests?
selfTest.a: It is a three-line triple loop over intermediate vertices with no heap, no settle logic and no stale entries: obviously correct by a separate argument, so agreement isolates Dijkstra's invariant rather than re-testing one implementation twice. Restrict weights to nonneg for the comparison.

selfTest.q: A shrunk Hypothesis failure shows a 3-vertex graph. What do you do?
selfTest.a: Keep it as a regression test, read off the violated assumption (disconnected input, parallel edges, self-loop), fix the solver or state the precondition, and re-run the full strategy.

selfTest.q: Why must comparisons share the instance?
selfTest.a: Graph shape, density and weight scale all move runtimes and even outputs; different instances confound the comparison. Same seed, same edge list, both algorithms, then compare.

units.title: Flow and matching at recognition depth
outcomes: State the max-flow min-cut theorem and explain how an equal-value cut certifies a claimed maximum flow.
Reduce bipartite matching to max flow with a source, a sink and unit capacities, and read a matching back from the flow.
Recognize flow-shaped problems (capacities, bottlenecks, conflict-free assignment) and name what a full implementation would still need.
units.why: Flows and matchings are recognition vocabulary at this stage: routing, assignment and cut problems recur across ML systems, and naming the reduction correctly is the transferable skill.

next.note: Reductions are the shared move: this unit reduces matching to flow the way later units reduce problems to shortest paths.
Assignment and matching structure reappears in data association and ranking evaluation.

study.title: Maximum Flows and Minimum Cuts, Chapter 10
study.locator: 10.1 Flows, 10.2 Cuts, 10.3 The Maxflow-Mincut Theorem and 10.4 Ford and Fulkerson's augmenting-path algorithm (printed pp. 328-336)

study.title: Flow applications including bipartite matching, Chapter 11
study.locator: 11.1 Edge-Disjoint Paths and 11.3 Bipartite Matching with the source-sink unit-capacity reduction (printed pp. 353-357)
study.depth: Read the reductions and state the constructions; skip implementing Dinic or push-relabel here.

focus: Recognition signals: capacities on edges plus a bottleneck question means flow; two-sided assignment with conflicts (left set, right set, allowed pairs) means bipartite matching.
The certificate is the cut: a flow of value \(F\) with a cut of capacity \(F\) is maximum by the theorem. Always exhibit both.
Bipartite matching is flow with unit capacities: source to left, allowed edges left to right, right to sink; integer flow of value \(k\) is a matching of size \(k\).
Explicit non-goals: residual-graph implementation at scale, Dinic or push-relabel, general (non-bipartite) matching and spectral methods stay in the section's leave-for-later list.
units.reproduce: From a blank file with the course Python (3.13.14), run Edmonds-Karp on \(n = 4\) with capacities [(0,1,3),(0,2,2),(1,2,1),(1,3,2),(2,3,3)] from 0 to 3 and report max flow 5. Exhibit the certifying cut (\(\{0\}\) versus \(\{1, 2, 3\}\)) with capacity 3 + 2 = 5.
traps: Augmenting without residual backward edges: the greedy path choice gets stuck below maximum because it cannot undo earlier flow. Backward edges with residual capacity are the algorithm, not an optimization.
Confusing bipartite check with bipartite matching: two-coloring decides a partition exists; matching finds the largest conflict-free edge set given one. LC 785 does not solve LC 1349.
Undirected edges as single arcs: an undirected edge of capacity c becomes two opposite arcs of capacity c. One arc forbids flow in the other direction and can silently lower the maximum.

selfTest.q: State the max-flow min-cut theorem and its use as a certificate.
selfTest.a: The value of a maximum \(s\)-\(t\) flow equals the capacity of a minimum \(s\)-\(t\) cut. A flow of value \(F\) plus a cut of capacity \(F\) proves optimality without trusting the solver: no flow can exceed any cut's capacity.

selfTest.q: Give the bipartite-matching-to-flow reduction exactly.
selfTest.a: Source \(s\) to each left vertex capacity 1, each allowed left-right pair capacity 1, each right vertex to sink \(t\) capacity 1. Integer max flow of value \(k\) saturates \(k\) disjoint pairs: a matching of size \(k\), and every matching yields such a flow.

selfTest.q: Why does LC 1349 admit a matching model?
selfTest.a: Color seats by column parity. Every conflict (left, right, upper-left, upper-right) joins an even column to an odd one, so the conflict graph is bipartite. The answer is a maximum independent set of free seats, which on a bipartite graph equals the number of free seats minus a maximum matching (Konig's theorem). A checkerboard coloring fails: diagonal neighbors share a color.

selfTest.q: What stays deliberately excluded, and why can you stop?
selfTest.a: Dinic, push-relabel, general-graph matching and spectral methods: the section checkpoint needs recognition plus a small checked construction, and the section's leave-for-later list names the rest.
